themes.definition: Grants of permission or mandates to use AI, instructions naming specific tasks AI should be used for, and how people configure what the AI then applies.
themes.what_is_set_out: DWP permits use on a condition: 'Approved AI tools and online AI tools that can be accessed on DWP devices may be used where there is a business requirement to do so'; the NAO's first maturity target is that 'People are encouraged and supported to use approved tools'. AI_Insights, on records management, asks senior leaders to 'Set a clear mandate' for knowledge and information management (KIM) and data teams to review and dispose of legacy content, notes that KIM professionals 'may need to seek a formal mandate', and prescribes specific uses: summarising and ranking drives, restoring corrupted dates, and highlighting passages that 'may fall under Freedom of Information Act exemptions'. In these uses people set what the AI applies: selection priorities used to 'prompt an LLM or train a classifier' (coder note), factors and weightings for value scoring, and exclusions for content under legal hold. More exploratory ideas include a shorter retention period for emails an AI sorts aside, daily LLM summaries kept instead of conversations, and an individual's permission for AI access to parts of their email. These are permissions rather than duties; the checks on outputs that go with them (human approval of disposal decisions) are set out under 'Decisions reserved to humans' and 'Human review and override of outputs'.
themes.holders: DWP users; NAO staff; senior leaders, KIM professionals and teams, and individual account holders (AI_Insights).

themes.theme: Organisations' own AI policies and governance
themes.definition: Requirements that a body write and maintain its own AI principles, acceptable-use policies and governance framework, and use them as the standard for AI use (a split of the starting code 'setting standards').
themes.what_is_set_out: Most documents expect each body to write its own AI rules and use them as the standard. UK174 recommends 'a simple set of top-level principles'; UK268 expects 'Internal guidelines on ethical AI use and associated legal risks' and project plans that reference internal AI policies; UK206 says 'all organisations should integrate robust organisational governance frameworks for AI systems'; UK266 asks whether there are 'documented principles on risk appetite, acceptable use, ethics, transparency and traceability' and guardrails such as acceptable-use policies. UK010 asks energy-sector stakeholders to set 'clear and proportionate guidelines and policies' and keep them up to date, and contains the only passage in the cell backed by a regulatory penalty: 'licensees or other regulated persons must ensure they have and maintain appropriate processes, systems and governance to ensure AI does not cause them to breach their regulatory obligations', enforceable by Ofgem with financial penalties (coder field). The NAO commits to 'a proportionate, enterprise-wide governance framework', seven principles, and mapping principles to policies and sourcing standards; DWP's Chief Security Officer owns and reviews the DWP AI Security Policy; and AI_Insights repeatedly makes 'your organisation’s policies' the test for coding assistants, generative AI sign-ups and development environments, with the Departmental Records Officer setting the disposal process. The content of these internal policies is left to each body.
themes.holders: Organisations and 'you' (UK174, UK268, UK206, UK266); energy-sector stakeholders, licensees and regulated persons (UK010); the NAO; DWP's Chief Security Officer; developers, staff and the Departmental Records Officer (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Mostly 'should' or questions in guidance; NAO commitments and roadmap actions; DWP policy. UK010 A1.17 is mandatory for licensees and regulated persons, with Ofgem able to impose financial penalties (the coder field cites up to 10%, text truncated).

themes.theme: Standards set elsewhere that AI use must meet
themes.definition: Requirements that AI tools comply with named cross-government or external standards set by bodies other than the user (a split of the starting code 'setting standards').
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 names several cross-government standards that apply to AI work: 'If you develop a service, you must use the government Service Standard'; a service 'must comply with the government’s Secure by Design principles before it can be deployed'; products and services must comply with 'the required standards as defined by standards development organisations (SDOs)' such as ISO; and the Green Book and the DDaT Playbook apply to spending and sourcing. AI_Insights places itself under the AI Playbook: its articles are to be used 'alongside the guidance in the Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government and your organisation’s policies', readers 'must consider all of these themes from the AI Playbook', and AI tools in records review are to be used 'in accordance with the principles set out in the AI Playbook'; it also names the Cloud First policy and the Service Standard as constraints on development environments. The NAO governs AI quality risks in financial audit 'through the system of quality management'. These passages name the standards without stating their content, and only Secure by Design is tied to a point in the tool's life (before deployment).

themes.theme: Central guidance as an adaptable baseline
themes.definition: How issuing bodies describe the status of their own guidance (a baseline, framework or set of principles) and leave adoption and detail to each department or team.
themes.what_is_set_out: Central documents mostly describe themselves as reference points and leave the operative decisions to each body. UK071 offers 'a minimum baseline of testing and evaluation for AI systems that impact the public, while allowing departments to adapt it', with modules departments 'can adopt, adapt, or extend'; UK099 'provides a set of principles and activities to guide'; UK133 (HM Treasury) 'outlines key principles of best practice'; UK216 (EHRC) says 'You should develop a checklist to fit your own circumstances'. UK174 defers to 'organisation-specific policies', AI_Insights says 'Policies and procedures will vary by team, department and organisation', and UK266 records that 'Individual departments and other public bodies remain responsible for security, data protection and assurance decisions within their own organisations'. The effect is that authority to set the operative standard sits with each body [inference]; no passage provides a way to check whether a department's adaptation still meets the baseline.
themes.holders: Issuers: the Cross-Government Testing Community (UK071), the Government Digital Service (UK099), HM Treasury's Evaluation Task Force (UK133), the EHRC (UK216). Adapters: departments, teams, organisations and public bodies.
themes.binding: Self-described as non-binding or adaptable (UK071 says it is not a checklist, per coder field); 'should' in UK216 and UK174; descriptive statements elsewhere.

themes.theme: Regulators and standards bodies as standard-setters
themes.definition: Allocation of authority to regulators, standards bodies and central government to set standards, guidance and expectations for AI developers and deployers in their remits, and the discretion they keep (a split of the starting code 'setting standards').
themes.what_is_set_out: UK139, guidance to regulators, leaves standard-setting to each regulator: 'It remains the responsibility of regulators to develop their own tools and guidance as they deem appropriate', the principles are 'voluntary and how they are considered is ultimately at regulators’ discretion', and regulators 'could' describe 'what a fair outcome from AI is', define safety and robustness for their remit, set an appropriate level of transparency, and place expectations on 'AI developers and deployers within regulators’ remits' (deployers include public bodies, per coder note), while regulators with technology-agnostic frameworks may judge the guidance inapplicable to them. UK206 restates that 'existing regulators will be responsible for interpreting and implementing the regulatory principles in their respective sectors' and gives standards bodies the role of developing 'commonly accepted standards that can be evaluated against'; UK207's roadmap prioritises management-system, risk-management and measurement standards 'that organisations can be certified against', and wants regulation to set 'assurable requirements'. Ofgem (UK010) 'sets out good practice for stakeholders to consider', will keep it under review, and states that the hierarchy of legal frameworks 'shall prevail' in any conflict; UK174 makes SDO-defined standards the reference for compliance. UK082 recommends that sponsor departments steer regulators towards 'enabling safe AI innovation', asks for clarity on how frontier models will be regulated, and floats a central body that could issue sandbox licences 'that override sector regulations'. Which regulator, if any, sets standards for public bodies' own use of AI is not stated in these passages.
themes.holders: Regulators (UK139, UK206, UK207); standards bodies such as ISO, IEC and BSI (UK206, UK207, UK174); Ofgem (UK010); government, sponsor departments and a proposed central body (UK082, UK206); government, regulators and private sector organisations together for the assurance market (UK207).
themes.binding: Voluntary and at regulators' discretion (UK139); descriptive role statements and aspirations (UK206, UK207); non-binding good-practice guidance, with Ofgem's existing statutory powers behind licence obligations (UK010); recommendations whose acceptance is not recorded (UK082). No new duties are created in these passages.

themes.definition: Requirements to allocate decision authority over AI to named boards, senior owners, teams or officers, and descriptions of who holds which decisions.
themes.what_is_set_out: Only a few documents name the holders of AI decisions. In the NAO, 'The Executive Team has overall accountability for AI strategy, risk appetite and key decisions', the NAO Board provides oversight, and the AI Governance Board provides 'delegated oversight, reviewing higher-risk and novel use cases, setting assurance expectations, and escalating issues'. UK071 gives go/no-go decisions to Senior Responsible Owners and governance boards and governance checkpoints to product managers; UK010 says 'Board members should be accountable, have the ultimate oversight, and own the role of delegating responsibilities', with oversight placed in the full board, an existing committee or a new AI committee, decision-makers given 'the necessary authority', and possibly an AI officer; UK268 describes a budgetary commissioner and a product owner who accepts deliverables. More often the documents require roles to be allocated without naming them: UK174 says 'you must define their roles and responsibilities' across the value chain and set out 'who has the authority to change and modify the code of the AI model'; UK099 says 'You must set out who is responsible at each stage of the project' and that accountable people need the 'authority, to implement necessary changes'; UK071, UK268 and AI_Insights ask for roles to be set early or in a lifecycle plan; UK136 points to multidisciplinary teams and process-based governance frameworks; UK206 asks for decisions 'at an appropriate level'. AI_Insights gives the KIM team 'complete control of the development, testing and deployment' of a purpose-built model, while information assurance colleagues or SROs 'can help to determine the feasibility of use', which is advice, not a stated power to approve or stop. Across the cell, coder notes repeatedly record that the decider is not stated even where a decision is required.

themes.theme: Scope: which bodies, tools and stages are covered
themes.definition: Statements fixing which organisations, users, tools and lifecycle stages fall within a document's requirements, including phasing.
themes.what_is_set_out: The ATRS documents (UK085, UK086) give the most exact scope in the cell, though they govern publication of records about tools rather than use of the tools. The requirement is mandatory for central government ('all government departments, and for ALBs which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public'), rolled out in two phases, excluding bodies outside the Freedom of Information Act, with the arm's-length bodies covered to be finalised by GDS 'with departments'. Tools are in scope if they 'have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or ... directly interact with the general public', once at 'Beta/Pilot or Production phase'; analytical models for broad policy-making are 'typically' out, and the body applies the public-effect test itself. The examples put an LLM that summarises public submissions for human decision-makers in scope and 'Ad-hoc usage of large language models, such as Microsoft Copilot being used by individual civil servants internally' out, so routine internal LLM use by officials falls outside the publication duty [inference]. DWP's policy covers employees and contractors using DWP equipment, 'All AI tools' (coder note), and suppliers and their third parties; UK133 excludes 'assessing the capabilities of AI systems against technical benchmarks or assessing the technical components'; UK136 is 'aimed at central government departments'; and UK268 cautions auditors against building alternative models beyond the audit institution's statutory tasks.
themes.holders: The Government Digital Service as issuer, working with departments on arm's-length body scope (UK085, UK086); organisations in scope, which apply the tests themselves; DWP as policy issuer; HM Treasury's Evaluation Task Force (UK133); the Office for AI (UK136); audit institution auditors (UK268, nearest actor).
themes.binding: ATRS: mandatory by policy for central government (non-statutory), with exclusions and examples marked as illustrative or 'typically'. DWP: mandatory by departmental policy. Scope statements in non-binding guidance otherwise.

themes.definition: Routes by which a body or user may be excused from a requirement, the grounds allowed, and who decides.
themes.what_is_set_out: Exemption decisions are mostly left to the body that would be exempted. Under the ATRS scope policy the organisation applies a hypothetical Freedom of Information request: exempt content 'should' be removed or de-sensitised before publication, and where the body would neither confirm nor deny the tool 'it would be inappropriate to publish the ATRS record at all'; personal-data concerns (FOIA section 40) 'should therefore not apply', and 'There is a need for care in applying commercial exemptions'. UK086 adds that redacting fields with an explanation 'is preferable to not publishing an ATRS record at all', and the ATRS template lets organisations leave the model and development-data sections blank for off-the-shelf models they have 'not trained, fine-tuned, validated, tested or applied refinement techniques to' (for example web-based LLMs). DWP lets a user with 'a strong justification' follow the ATRS exemption process and allows 'An exception to policy' where a business case can be made, without naming who grants either; UK139 lets regulators with technology-agnostic frameworks decide for themselves that its guidance does not apply. No passage provides external review or notification of these exemption decisions (coder notes), and the off-the-shelf exemption means that for unmodified vendor models no model performance or development data is recorded [inference, coder note].
themes.holders: Organisations in ATRS scope, deciding for themselves; the ATRS team and the Government Digital Service setting the rules (UK085, UK087); DWP users, with the grantor not stated; regulators with technology-agnostic frameworks (UK139).
themes.binding: ATRS exemption rules are mandatory policy for central government (non-statutory), with the off-the-shelf exemption permissive ('may leave ... blank'); the DWP exception route is 'may be requested'; the UK139 exemption is at regulators' discretion.

absences: Every starting code for Decision-making has passages in this cell: whether a tool is used, approved, paused or stopped; overriding outputs; setting priorities, direction and standards; issuing mandates; deciding scope and exemptions; and appointing who decides. What a reader would expect but the passages do not provide: (1) a named decision-maker for pausing, rolling back or decommissioning a tool; every such passage leaves it unstated, and the only stops that need no decider are the automatic rollbacks in the AI_Insights bias guidance and end users switching a model off in their own account. (2) Defined thresholds: 'too high', 'unacceptable', 'sufficiently safe', 'significant', 'critical' and 'materially' are undefined, and the only numbers are spend thresholds and an illustrative '90% accuracy'. (3) Any body outside the deploying organisation with power to approve, pause or stop a public body's AI tool: approval sits inside DWP, the NAO and other bodies, the ATRS team gates only publication of a record, and regulators' remit over public-sector deployers is not described. (4) Review of a body's own ATRS scope and exemption decisions. (5) Rules that route outputs to a human by confidence score, sampling or error rate, and any decision criterion on consistency or repeatability of outputs, prompt or configuration control, or fixing model versions; model versions appear only as something to roll back to, or as a change that triggers re-testing. (6) Consequences for skipping a gate, apart from DWP's discipline route, Ofgem's penalties for licensees, and the statutory consequences restated from data protection and equality law. (7) The relationship between DWP's Digital Design Authority and its AI Delivery Board.
cross_cutting: This cell is dominated by the decision whether to use AI and on what terms, framed mostly as tests the deploying body applies to itself (need, alternatives, benefit against risk, its own risk appetite), and by the passing of standard-setting downwards, to each organisation's own policies and to regulators' discretion, rather than by central rules. It is binding mainly where existing law or existing controls are restated (UK GDPR's human decision-maker for legal-status decisions, the equality duty, human rights, spend controls, Secure by Design) and where one department writes its own policy (DWP's named boards, data approvals, change approvals and a named prohibited tool); the ATRS is mandatory but governs what is published about a tool, not whether it is used, and lets bodies decide their own exemptions. Elsewhere 'must' appears often in non-statutory guidance with no stated consequence, and the most pro-adoption text (UK082) is an independent report whose acceptance is not recorded, sitting in unresolved tension with the 'consider not using AI at all' line in UK174 and UK099 [inference]. Holders are usually 'you' or 'the organisation'; named holders (DWP's boards, the NAO's Executive Team and AI Governance Board, SROs and governance boards in UK071, KIM teams in AI_Insights) are the exception, and coder notes repeatedly record that whoever decides go/no-go, rollback or decommissioning is not stated. The thin areas are who stops a tool, what the thresholds are, and any authority over a public body's AI use from outside that body. On checking AI outputs, the cell sets out three mechanisms: human review, approval or override for high-risk, significant or critical decisions (statutory only in UK174's legal-status rule, otherwise guidance); acceptance criteria, metrics and bias thresholds that each body fixes in advance and against which go/no-go and change decisions are made (UK268, UK071, AI_Insights), with numbers given only as illustrations; and, in one document (AI_Insights on LLM bias), automated deployment gates and automatic rollback on threshold breaches. Which cases reach a human is set by risk category rather than by confidence scores or sampling, and consistency or repeatability of outputs, prompts or configuration, and model versions enter only as triggers for re-testing and re-approval after a change (UK268, UK071, DWP), not as acceptance criteria.
